title: Aldehydes and Ketones I
description: Explore carbonyl electrophilicity, addition products, and oxidation–reduction.
objectives: Identify hydrates, hemiacetals, acetals, imines, and enamines

sources.label: Supplied Kaplan curriculum: Chapter 6; section scope checked against local body and summary
IUPAC Gold Book, acetals (search-index definition inspected; direct page fetch unavailable)

cards.rule: The carbonyl is polarized Cδ+–Oδ−. A nucleophile attacks carbon while the pi pair shifts to oxygen; protonation can then give an alcohol. Aldehydes are generally less crowded and less electron-rich than comparable ketones, so they often add nucleophiles more readily.
cards.cue: Attack C; move pi electrons to O; then handle proton transfers. Aldehydes use -al, or -carbaldehyde when CHO is attached to a ring; ketones use -one. Use oxo- for a subordinate carbonyl. Methanal/formaldehyde, ethanal/acetaldehyde, propanal/propionaldehyde, butanal/butyraldehyde and pentanal/valeraldehyde are common name pairs; propanone is acetone.
cards.trap: Neutral aldehydes and ketones can accept hydrogen bonds but lack an O–H donor. Do not draw five bonds to carbon when a nucleophile adds. A planar carbonyl can be attacked from either face. At comparable mass and shape, boiling points often follow alkane < aldehyde/ketone < alcohol; this is a trend, not a universal ordering across unrelated molecules.
cards.app: A chiral environment can favor one face; without such bias, addition that creates a single new stereocenter often yields a racemic mixture.

steps.label: 1. Find the electrophile
steps.text: The C=O carbon is trigonal planar and electron poor. Oxygen is electron rich.

steps.label: 2. Move the pi pair
steps.text: The purple curved arrow shows the carbonyl pi pair moving toward oxygen during nucleophilic attack. This arrow is one part of an addition mechanism; the incoming nucleophile is described in the lesson rather than drawn here.

lessons.label: Hydrates, hemiacetals, and acetals
lessons.title: Hydrates, hemiacetals, and acetals
lessons.tag: Distinguish OH from OR on the same carbon

cards.rule: A hydrate has two OH groups on one carbon. In traditional terminology, aldehyde-derived hemiacetals have OH, OR, H and R at the former carbonyl carbon; further acid-catalyzed reaction gives acetals with two OR groups, H and R. Ketone-derived counterparts have two carbon groups and are called hemiketals (OH + OR) and ketals (two OR). Broad IUPAC acetal/hemiacetal classes also include the ketone-derived compounds. Equilibria depend on water/alcohol activities.
cards.cue: Two OH = hydrate; OH + OR = hemiacetal; two OR = acetal. Ketone-derived examples are also called hemiketals/ketals.
cards.trap: Acetal formation requires acid catalysis; base alone does not turn OH− into a good leaving group. Cyclic sugar hemiacetals can be stable because intramolecular ring formation is favorable.
cards.app: Monosaccharides cyclize through hemiacetal or hemiketal formation. The new anomeric center can have two configurations. Acetal/ketal protection can preserve a carbonyl during many basic or hydride reactions, including suitable LiAlH4 conditions. Aqueous acid restores the carbonyl; compatibility must be checked for the whole substrate.

steps.label: 1. Identify a hemiacetal
steps.text: This carbon bears both OH and OCH3, along with methyl and H. It is a hemiacetal from ethanal and methanol.

steps.label: 2. Compare a ketal
steps.text: This separate ketone-derived example is a ketal: two OCH3 groups and two carbon groups surround the central carbon. It is not the direct next product of the ethanal hemiacetal in step 1. Aqueous-acid hydrolysis regenerates a ketone.

steps.label: 3. Compare a hydrate
steps.text: Here both oxygen substituents are OH: a geminal diol. The equilibrium does not equally favor hydrates for every carbonyl.

cards.rule: A primary amine condenses with an aldehyde or ketone to form an imine after addition, proton transfers, and water loss. A secondary amine can form an enamine when an alpha H is available. Related nitrogen reagents form oximes (hydroxylamine), hydrazones (hydrazine derivatives), and semicarbazones (semicarbazide). Cyanide addition followed by protonation forms a cyanohydrin and creates a C–C bond. Ammonia can also give an imine under suitable condensation conditions. An imine with an available alpha H can interconvert with an enamine tautomer by proton and double-bond relocation. Secondary-amine condensation proceeds through an iminium ion and alpha deprotonation; no N–H remains at that intermediate.
cards.cue: Primary amine → C=N; secondary amine + alpha H → C=C–N. Cyanide adds its carbon.
cards.trap: Too much acid protonates the amine and suppresses its nucleophilicity. Enamine formation needs an alpha hydrogen. Do not attach cyanide through nitrogen in a standard cyanohydrin product.
cards.app: Schiff-base (imine) intermediates help enzymes reorganize electron density; nitrogen chemistry is a bridge to amino-acid metabolism.

steps.label: 1. Imine bond
steps.text: The C=N bond replaces the starting C=O after condensation with a primary amine. This connectivity drawing does not assign E/Z about C=N.

steps.label: 2. Enamine bond
steps.text: An enamine has N attached to a C=C system. The nitrogen lone pair is conjugated with the double bond, giving nucleophilic carbon character. The displayed imine and enamine are separate examples with different substituents and formulas, not a tautomeric pair.

steps.label: 3. Cyanohydrin carbon count
steps.text: Acetone cyanohydrin contains a new C–C bond between the former carbonyl carbon and the nitrile carbon. The nitrile N is triple-bonded to that new carbon.

cards.rule: Aldehydes can be oxidized to carboxylic acids; ordinary ketones resist analogous oxidation without C–C cleavage. NaBH4 and LiAlH4 reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Hydride adds first, then oxygen is protonated in workup or by the medium. Suitable aqueous KMnO4 or Cr(VI) reagents (CrO3/acid or dichromate/acid) oxidize aldehydes. Tollens reagent is ammoniacal Ag(I), which is reduced to silver while an aldehyde becomes carboxylate in the basic medium; acid workup gives the acid. H2O2 can oxidize aldehydes under suitable conditions. Anhydrous PCC is commonly chosen to make aldehydes from primary alcohols while limiting overoxidation; it is not the only selective reagent.
cards.trap: Do not predict an alkane from ordinary hydride reduction of C=O. The oxygen remains in the alcohol. A positive aldehyde oxidation test is contextual evidence, not a complete structural identification. Tollens reagent is not a general primary-alcohol oxidant. Water, pH, workup and other oxidizable groups affect selectivity.
cards.app: Biological NADH-dependent carbonyl reductions transfer a hydride equivalent; the enzyme can control stereochemistry.

steps.label: 1. Aldehyde substrate
steps.text: Ethanal has a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, allowing ordinary oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

steps.label: 2. Oxidized product
steps.text: Ethanoic acid retains the two-carbon skeleton and adds a carbon–oxygen bond overall.

steps.label: 3. Reduced product
steps.text: The reduction product ethanol retains the same oxygen but has a single C–O bond and more C–H bonding.

exercises.label: Follow nucleophilic addition
exercises.title: Follow nucleophilic addition

stages.prompt: Select the atom attacked by a carbon nucleophile.
stages.explanation: The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon.
hints: Locate the positively polarized end of C=O.
Carbon is less electronegative than oxygen.

stages.prompt: As the new sigma bond forms, the C=O pi pair moves to…
stages.explanation: Moving the pi pair to O prevents carbon from exceeding an octet.
hints: Count the carbon bonds during attack.
O can carry the resulting negative charge.

stages.prompt: The immediate former-carbonyl geometry becomes approximately…
stages.explanation: Addition replaces the pi bond and gives four sigma directions around carbon.
hints: Count electron domains after addition.
Four directions correspond to sp³-like geometry.

exercises.summary: Nucleophilic addition changes planar C=O into a tetrahedral center.
exercises.context: The canvas retains the starting ethanal to trace one electron-flow step. The incoming nucleophile and tetrahedral product are not drawn.

exercises.label: Read oxygen substituents
exercises.title: Read oxygen substituents

stages.prompt: Select the carbon bearing two oxygen substituents.
stages.explanation: B is the former carbonyl carbon.
hints: Trace both C–O bonds to their shared carbon.
The O atoms are C and D.

stages.prompt: One OH and one OR on that carbon identify a…
stages.explanation: A hemiacetal has both OH and OR.
hints: Inspect whether each oxygen also has a carbon substituent.
One oxygen is OH; the other links to methyl.

stages.prompt: Converting it to an acetal with alcohol is favored by…
options: Acid catalysis and removal of water
stages.explanation: Acid enables water departure; removing water shifts the equilibrium toward acetal.
hints: Water is a product of acetal formation.
Apply Le Châtelier’s principle.

exercises.summary: Hemiacetal: OH + OR on the same carbon.

exercises.label: Track the new carbon bond
exercises.title: Track the new carbon bond

stages.prompt: Select the nitrile carbon added by cyanide.
stages.explanation: E is the carbon triple-bonded to N and bonded to the former carbonyl carbon.
hints: Cyanide adds through carbon.
Find the carbon endpoint of C≡N.

stages.prompt: How many carbons are in the cyanohydrin?
stages.explanation: Acetone supplies three carbons and cyanide supplies one.
hints: Count carbon atoms, not total atoms.
Include the nitrile carbon.

stages.prompt: Select both carbon endpoints of the new C–C bond formed by cyanide addition.
stages.explanation: B is the former carbonyl carbon and E is the cyanide-derived carbon. The new sigma bond joins B and E.
hints: Trace the single bond from the nitrile carbon toward the OH-bearing center.
Select two carbon atoms; the nitrogen endpoint of C≡N is not part of the new C–C bond.

exercises.summary: Cyanohydrin formation joins the cyanide carbon to the former carbonyl carbon, adding one carbon overall.

stages.prompt: Select the carbonyl carbon receiving hydride.
hints: Hydride is the nucleophile.
Attack the electron-poor carbon.

stages.prompt: After protonation, the product is a…
stages.explanation: The alcohol-bearing carbon retains its two methyl substituents.
hints: Count carbon neighbors of the new C–OH carbon.
No C–C bonds are added or removed.
Retain the three-carbon chain.
Place OH at the central carbon.
